briefing: Welcome to dispatch. Three city blocks stand in a row with two alarm stations between them. Our arsonist, Noise, only lights red fires here (X errors). A station rings when exactly one of its two blocks is burning. Read the alarms, then send one red crew.

debrief.detectable: At least one station is still ringing: either the original fire is still burning, or a crew lit a new one on a safe block. Each station watches two blocks; the burning block is the one every ringing station shares.
debrief.logical-error: Every alarm is quiet, yet the pattern left behind is a full logical flip (XXX). A crew sent to a safe block starts a fire of its own, so silence alone never proves safety. Compare your dispatch with the alarms in the replay.
debrief.success: Both stations rang, and block 1 is the only block they share. Your red crew met the fire head on, and two red flames cancel (X·X = I). The logical qubit is safe.

title: First Alarm

training.caption: A red fire (X) on block 0. Station Z0 watches blocks 0 and 1, sees exactly one fire, and rings. Station Z1 watches blocks 1 and 2, sees none, and stays quiet.

briefing: Fires never spread on their own; gates carry them. A CNOT copies a red fire (X) from its control to its target, and copies a blue fire (Z) from its target back to its control. Watch the training runs, then predict where the fires end up and send crews there.

debrief.detectable: This lesson has no alarm stations, so a ringing alarm cannot occur here.
debrief.logical-error: There are no alarm stations on bare wires, so any fire you missed, or lit by mistake, acts directly on the data. Check both colours on each block: a Y fire needs both a red and a blue component to put it out.
debrief.success: Red went forward and blue went backward at the same time, so XZ became YY: a red-and-blue fire on both blocks. Your crews matched every component, and nothing remains.

title: Red Forward / Blue Backward

training.caption: Red forward: a red fire (X) on the control copies onto the target. XI becomes XX.
Blue backward: a blue fire (Z) on the target copies onto the control. IZ becomes ZZ.

briefing: A Hadamard gate swaps colours: red becomes blue and blue becomes red, on its own wire only. Combined with a CNOT, a single fire can change colour, copy itself, and change colour again. Follow the circuit one gate at a time.

debrief.detectable: This lesson has no alarm stations, so a ringing alarm cannot occur here.
debrief.logical-error: One of the fires ended up with a different colour, or on a different block, than you dispatched for. Replay the circuit: H swaps colours only on its own wire, and CNOT copies red forward and blue backward.
debrief.success: ZI turned into XI at the first Hadamard, copied forward to XX through the CNOT, and the final Hadamard on block 1 turned that copy blue: XZ. You traced the whole path.

title: Color Switch

training.caption: Colour switch: a Hadamard turns the red fire (X) on block 0 into a blue one (Z). XI becomes ZI.
Blue turns red at the H, then red copies forward through the CNOT. ZI becomes XX.

briefing: Welcome to the surface code district: nine blocks and eight alarm stations. Red stations (Z checks, diamonds) notice red fires; blue stations (X checks, squares) notice blue fires. This time the fire is hidden. Read the alarms and send one crew.

debrief.detectable: Alarms are still ringing. A red crew on a block that was not burning starts a new fire, and a blue crew cannot put out a red fire at all. Match the crew colour to the station type, then find the block that every ringing station shares.
debrief.logical-error: The alarms went quiet, but the pattern left behind acts as a logical operator on the encoded qubit. With one hidden fire and one crew this cannot happen in this district; Silent Failure shows when it does.
debrief.success: Stations Z0 and Z1 both rang, and block 4 is the only block they share. One red crew, fire out, logical qubit safe.

title: Blind Dispatch

training.caption: A red fire (X) on block 0 rings only station Z0, which watches blocks 0, 1, 3 and 4. A fire on block 3 alone would ring exactly the same station, so a crew sent to block 3 is just as good a fix: the two dispatches differ by a stabilizer (the X2 station's own pattern), which the code does not care about.

briefing: Two fires this time, and they may be different colours. Red stations only ever notice red fires and blue stations only blue ones, so read the two alarm maps separately. You have two crews; a mixed crew (Y) counts as one crew on one block.

debrief.detectable: Some stations are still ringing. Remember that a red station never sees a blue fire: solve the red alarms and the blue alarms as two separate puzzles, one crew colour each.
debrief.logical-error: Every alarm is quiet but the leftover pattern is a logical operator: your crews and the fires together form a chain across the district instead of cancelling. The replay shows where the chain runs.
debrief.success: Red stations Z0 and Z2 share only block 1. Blue station X1 rang alone, which points at its boundary pair, blocks 6 and 7; a blue crew on either one works, because the two choices differ by a stabilizer. Two colours, two fires, both out.

title: Two Kinds of Trouble

briefing: Only one alarm is ringing: station Z0. Dispatch protocol is simple: send the smallest crew that silences every station. Make the call, and then we will look at what really happened.

debrief.detectable: Stations are still ringing, so the smallest silencing crew was not sent. Protocol for a lone Z0 alarm is one red crew on block 0 or block 3; replay the alarms and compare.
debrief.logical-error: That was the optimal call. Only Z0 rang, and the best explanation of one alarm is one fire, on block 0 or block 3. But Noise lit two fires, on blocks 1 and 2. Your crew plus those two fires form X on blocks 0, 1 and 2: a logical X, which every station sees as an even count and so cannot detect. This code has distance 3: any single fire is always fixed, but two fires can fool any dispatcher, because no alarm pattern justified sending crews to blocks 1 and 2. That is why real machines use bigger codes.
debrief.success: You put out both fires, on blocks 1 and 2. Honest question: how did you know? The alarms were identical to a single fire on block 0 or block 3, so this was a guess that happened to land. Protocol would still send one crew to block 0.

title: Silent Failure
